newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower on November housing jump.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower on November housing jump.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Monday, hurt by a stronger-than-expected jump in November U.S. housing starts but scarcely affected by the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady.
Prices cut their steepest losses mid-afternoon after the Lynch, Jones & Ryan retail sales index showed store sales running slower than expected the first two weeks of December.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 97-28/32, down 15/32, its yield up to 6.66 percent versus 6.63 percent at Monday's close.
"The market got knocked down by the housing number," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston.
The government reported that housing starts jumped to an annualized 1.514 million in November, up from an annualized rate of 1.386 million in October.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a bounce to 1.390 million.
Analysts tied the brisk activity in the housing sector to stimulus provided by the lower interest rates that prevailed during early autumn.

"If you expected the summer rise in interest rates to curtail activity, the (bond) rally (and lower rates) in the fall could have rejuvenated builders' expectations," said Kevin Flanagan, market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Interest-rate changes over the last several months have been market driven and not due to any official moves in Fed monetary policy.
That held true again on Tuesday when Fed policy makers gathered at a regularly scheduled meeting and left interest rates unchanged, an outcome widely anticipated on Wall Street.

"The expectation was so widespread on the Street that the Fed would leave policy unchanged that investors were more focused on the Redbook report than on the Fed," said Patrick Dimick, trader and bond market strategist at UBS Securities.
Traders said the market got support at 6.69 percent on the 30-year bond yield and "very good support" at 112 on the March T-bond futures contract.
Buying in that area inspired some players to cover shorts, a factor that helped to bring the market up from its lowest levels of the session, traders said.
Analysts said supply concerns also weighed on prices. The Treasury will sell $18.25 billion in two-year notes on Wednesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Thursday.

On a when-issued basis, the new two-year notes to be sold on Wednesday ended with a 5.855 percent yield on Tuesday. The five-year notes to be sold on Thursday finished with a when-issued yield of 6.1875 percent.

Short-term rates rose sharply on Tuesday. Three-month Treasury bill rates rose eight basis points to 4.90 percent. Six-month bill rates rose five basis points to 5.07 percent. Year bill rates rose four basis points to 5.23 percent.
Two-year notes fell 3/32 to 99-18/32, yielding 5.86 percent.
Five-year notes dropped 8/32 to 98-23/32 to yield 6.18 percent.
Ten-year notes skidded 11/32 to 100-18/32 to end with a 6.42 percent yield.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679
